You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- print_test(params, parts): optional. If you need to know whether something is going to work but you're not sure, ask the person to print a test of it before you hand in the final design, so you both save time and filament. They print it and tell you how each piece came out.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 12 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

The roller wheel on my sliding closet door snapped. I've got two 608 skateboard bearings and an M8 bolt I could use. Could I 3D print a new wheel that spins on the bolt? The old one was about 50 mm across and about 16 mm wide.

I still need to pin down the gap width in the bracket where the wheel sits, whether the track is flat or a V groove, and how long a bolt I can use. I'll measure those before settling the design.

Each bearing is 7 mm wide, seated from either face, which leaves a 2 mm center web. The bearing inner races will be clamped by spacers on the bolt, while the wheel turns on the outer races, so I'm checking whether the 2 mm web with a bore around 10 mm holds up.

I'm checking whether a 14 mm bore in the web clears the roughly 12 mm inner race while still giving the outer race a shoulder to seat against. The bigger issue is axial: with 7 mm pockets the bearings sit flush with the wheel faces, so the bracket would rub the rotating outer race, and I'm considering recessing the pockets slightly to avoid that.

I'm checking whether printed spacers could take the clamping load instead of the washers, since the washers would otherwise rub the rotating outer race. A sleeve with an outer diameter of about 10 mm would sit on the inner race without touching the outer race, and I'm weighing how far it should extend past the bearing face.

I'm weighing whether a coupon print is worth the time to check the 22 mm pocket fit before committing to the full wheel. The spacer length still depends on the bracket gap, which I can't measure from here, so I'm leaning toward printing a small test piece first.

I'm going to print a coupon with three pocket diameters, 22.0, 22.2, and 22.4 mm, to find the right press fit before committing to the full wheel. The design parameters are settled: 50 mm OD, 16 mm wide, 22 mm bearings, an 8 mm bore to match the bolt, and a 0.15 mm clearance. I'll print it flat with the pockets facing the bed and a small chamfer on the openings to handle elephant foot.

Next I'm settling the spacers and hardware: printed sleeves around 10 mm OD and 8.4 mm ID, with the length left as a parameter since the bracket gap is unknown. I'll note that washers can take up any remaining slack, and list the bolt and nut as hardware to source rather than fixing a length I can't verify.

I'm deciding on the hardware for the assembly: an ISO 4762 M8x40 socket bolt with a matching M8 lock nut, since I can't confirm the bracket gap from here. Next I'm settling the coupon, a small plate with three pockets at 22.0, 22.15, and 22.3 mm to check the press fit before printing the full wheel.

I'm going to test the pocket fit with three small coupon discs, each about 30 mm across with a 3 mm deep pocket, so I can print them as one part with the tolerance check built in.
